subtype: Approach: letting go of a small item after a fair search [Revision]
passage: Amandeep's pink sharpener, the cheap one from the corner shop, was gone. She checked her pencil box, the side pockets of her bag, and under her bench in the Delhi classroom. She asked Damini, her deskmate, and then the class monitor. Nobody had seen it. Twenty minutes of the free period had already gone, and her science diagram was only half done. Amandeep looked at the clock, then at her blunt pencil. It's a small thing, she thought. Not worth the whole period. "Damini, can I borrow yours?" That evening, when Papa brought home a new one, she wrote AMAN on it in marker before it went into her box.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep look for the sharpener?
qa.a: In her pencil box, the side pockets of her bag and under her bench.

qa.q: What was going through Amandeep's mind as she looked at the clock and the blunt pencil?
qa.a: She felt a bit annoyed about the loss but calm enough to decide a cheap sharpener wasn't worth losing the whole period.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do if things keep going missing?
qa.a: Keep the sharpener in one fixed pocket of her pencil box; writing her name on the new one also helps it come back if it's lost again.

qa.q: How might Damini see being asked to lend her sharpener?
qa.a: Damini had already been asked about the lost one, so lending hers is an easy way to help Amandeep get back to the diagram.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after a proper search and asking around, decides a cheap sharpener isn't worth more time, borrows one and names the next.

subtype: Approach: letting go of a small item after a fair search [Revision]
passage:
"Lakshmi, have you seen my sharpener? The little blue one?"
"No. Did you check your bag?"
"Bag, pencil box, under the table, even the dustbin. I asked Sir too."
"Then it's gone."
Arohi chewed her lip. "It was only a small one. But it was mine."
"The test starts in ten minutes."
Arohi looked at the clock, then at her blunt pencil. "Okay. I've looked properly. It's not worth missing the test." She held out her hand. "Can I borrow yours?"
"Here. Give it back, though!"
"I will. And the next one I buy, I'm writing AROHI on it in big letters."
Lakshmi grinned. "In glitter pen?"
"Obviously."

qa.q: Where had Arohi already looked?
qa.a: Her bag, her pencil box, under the table and even the dustbin.

qa.q: Why did Arohi chew her lip?
qa.a: She felt a little sad and reluctant to give the sharpener up because it was hers, even though it was only a small one.

qa.q: Which part of Arohi's approach worked best, and why?
qa.a: Stopping after a proper search so she didn't lose test time; borrowing solves today, and the name will help next time.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Arohi's decision?
qa.a: Lakshmi reminded Arohi about the test and hands over a sharpener at once, so Lakshmi seems to find the decision sensible and even jokes about the glitter pen.

grounding: Illustrates a girl letting go of a small lost sharpener after a fair search, borrowing one and planning to name the next.

subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Last Monday I came home from school with a mountain of Class 5 homework, or that's how it felt. I flopped on the bed and wanted to cry. Then I remembered something Ma'am once said, and took a page. I wrote: maths sums, Hindi paragraph, drawing of the water cycle. Next to each I guessed a time. Sums, ten minutes; there were only six. Hindi, twenty, because I'm slow at writing. Drawing, thirty, because I like to colour properly. I added them up. One hour. Only one hour! Dhruv, my little brother, peeped in. "Binita didi, will you play?" I said, "After one hour." And I meant it.

qa.q: How much time did Binita guess for the drawing?
qa.a: Thirty minutes, because Binita likes to colour properly.

qa.q: How did Binita feel before and after adding up the times?
qa.a: Binita felt overwhelmed at first, as if the homework were a mountain, then relieved and more confident once the total came to one hour 😊

qa.q: What else could Binita try if her guesses turn out wrong?
qa.a: She could check the clock after each task and adjust her next guess; the list still helps because it breaks the work into clear pieces.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Binita's plan?
qa.a: Dhruv wanted to play straight away, but 'after one hour' gives him a clear time to wait for, which is easier than a vague 'later'.

grounding: Shows a Class 5 child listing three homework tasks, guessing a time for each, and finding the total is one hour, which makes the work feel finite.

subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
passage: Tutor's note, Thursday. Devika arrived in a flap, saying she had "too much" homework and would never finish. I asked her to write it all down instead of worrying about it. She made a list: maths sums, Hindi paragraph, map drawing. Then, without my help, she wrote a guess beside each: 10, 20, 30 minutes. She added them under her breath. "That's one hour. That's not too much." Her shoulders dropped. Nandini, who sits next to her, asked if she could copy the idea for her own homework. Devika finished five minutes over her guess. I'll suggest this to her parents at pickup.

qa.q: How long over her guess did Devika finish?
qa.a: She finished five minutes over her guess.

qa.q: What do Devika's dropping shoulders suggest?
qa.a: She felt relieved and calmer once the total came to one hour, after arriving flustered about 'too much' homework.

qa.q: What might the note-writer suggest if Devika's guesses are often off?
qa.a: Write the real time beside each guess, so her estimates improve; the list already turned a scary pile into a clear hour.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Devika's list?
qa.a: Nandini finds it useful enough to ask to copy the idea for her own homework.

grounding: Illustrates a child listing her homework tasks, estimating ten, twenty and thirty minutes, and seeing the total is only one hour.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest subject first while fresh [Action]
passage:
"Mohit, snack's done. Homework?"
"Yes, Ganga didi. Maths first."
"Maths? You always do the map first."
"The map is just colouring. The word problems need my brain." He opened his notebook. "Right now my brain is awake."
Twenty minutes later: "Didi, is a dozen twelve?"
"Twelve."
"Then the farmer has thirty-six mangoes." He ticked it.
Forty minutes later he yawned, pulled out the map and his crayons. "Now I can be sleepy. Colouring doesn't need thinking."
Ganga laughed. "Who taught you this?"
"Me. Last week I did maths at night and got four wrong."

qa.q: How many mangoes did the farmer have in Mohit's word problem?
qa.a: Thirty-six mangoes.

qa.q: Why did Mohit choose maths first?
qa.a: He felt fresh and confident after his snack and wanted to use that for the hard word problems, remembering the four wrong answers from last week.

qa.q: What else could Mohit add to his plan?
qa.a: A short break between maths and the map; hardest-first works because his head is clearest right after the snack.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Mohit's new order?
qa.a: Ganga is surprised and amused, since he always did the map first, and asks who taught him.

grounding: Shows a boy doing maths word problems straight after his snack while his head is clear, and leaving map colouring for when he is tired.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest subject first while fresh [Action]
passage: This year I changed how I do homework, and it was my own idea. I used to start with the easy stuff, like colouring the map of India, and leave maths word problems for last. By then my eyes would be closing, and I'd read the same question five times. Now I eat my poha, drink some water, and open maths straight away while my head feels clear. Yesterday there were eight word problems about trains and tanks. I finished them in thirty-five minutes. Then, when I was yawning, I coloured the rivers blue and the hills brown. You don't need a sharp brain to colour. Sarita, my elder sister, said, "Suraj, you're finishing before me now, bhai."

qa.q: How many word problems did Suraj do yesterday?
qa.a: Eight word problems about trains and tanks.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when he used to leave maths for last?
qa.a: Suraj felt tired and frustrated, with eyes closing and reading the same question five times.

qa.q: What could Suraj try on days when there's no map, only more hard work?
qa.a: Still do the hardest task first and save anything routine, like neat copying, for the sleepy end of the evening.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Suraj's change?
qa.a: Sarita notices that Suraj now finishes before her, and seems surprised and perhaps a little impressed.

grounding: Illustrates a boy starting with maths word problems while his head is clear and leaving map colouring for when he is tired.

subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]
passage: Study hour at the girls' hostel ran from six to half past eight. Himani spread out her homework and chose the nicest bits first: a poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing. The glitter pens came out. Urmila, at the next desk, was already scratching away at fractions. By eight the poster was beautiful and the poem neat, but eight sums still waited. Himani's eyes kept closing. She rushed through them, guessing at two. Next day the teacher returned the notebook with three red crosses and a note: 'Careless. Were you tired?' Himani stared at the crosses, cheeks hot.

qa.q: What were the first two things Himani did during study hour?
qa.a: A poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she stared at the red crosses?
qa.a: Her hot cheeks suggest she felt embarrassed and disappointed, since the mistakes came from rushing while sleepy.

qa.q: What would you change first in Himani's plan?
qa.a: Do the fractions at six while fresh, and keep the poster and poem for the end when she's tired; the fun parts need less thinking.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Himani's evening?
qa.a: Urmila did the fractions first, so Urmila might admire the poster but wonder why the hard sums were left so late.

grounding: Shows a girl doing the pleasant drawing and copying first, leaving hard sums until eight when she is sleepy and rushes them with mistakes.

subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]
passage: I share a study table with my cousin Charu in the holidays, so I watched how her evening went. At five she pulled out the fun things first: a rainforest picture to colour, then a page of neat copying. She hummed, sharpened every colour pencil, and drew a parrot nobody had asked for. At eight, Pallavi Aunty called, "Dinner in ten minutes. Are the sums done?" Charu went quiet. She opened the maths notebook, rubbed her eyes, and wrote answers very fast. I saw her write 56 for 7 × 9. I don't know if she noticed. She shut the notebook and yawned all through dinner.

qa.q: What did Charu draw that nobody had asked for?
qa.a: A parrot.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when Pallavi Aunty asked about the sums?
qa.a: Going quiet suggests she felt worried and a bit guilty, realising the hard part was still left at eight.

qa.q: What could Charu try the next evening?
qa.a: Start the maths at five while she's alert and colour the rainforest after; a sleepy slip like 56 for 7 × 9 is then less likely.

qa.q: How might Pallavi Aunty see the evening?
qa.a: Pallavi Aunty probably expected the sums done before dinner, and may be surprised by a yawning child and rushed answers.

grounding: Illustrates a girl doing the fun colouring and copying first, then rushing the hard sums sleepily at eight and making mistakes.

subtype: Approach: pushing it off until just before bedtime [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Charu, and I share a room with my brother Chetan, so I saw the whole thing. After school he said, "Science is only one diagram, I've got loads of time," and went to play cricket in the lane till dark. Then cartoons, then dinner, then more cartoons. At nine he opened his notebook and read the question: draw and label the human digestive system. He counted the labels. Fourteen. His face crumpled and he started crying. "Papa, it'll take an hour!" Papa came and sat with him, yawning, sharpening pencils while Chetan drew. I can't say what Chetan was thinking earlier, but at nine he didn't look like he had loads of time.

qa.q: How many labels did the diagram need?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling at nine when he read the question?
qa.a: His face crumpled and he cried, so he felt panicked and upset, realising the diagram would take an hour.

qa.q: What could Chetan do differently tomorrow?
qa.a: Look at the homework right after school and do the diagram before cricket, since 'loads of time' vanished once he started playing.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa at nine o'clock?
qa.a: Papa is tired and yawning but still sits and helps, so Chetan's delay has become Papa's late night too.

grounding: Shows a boy telling himself there is plenty of time, playing and watching cartoons, then crying at nine when the diagram needs an hour.

subtype: Approach: pushing it off until just before bedtime [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday. Dhruv's teacher set one weekend task: a labelled diagram of a plant cell. "Two whole days," Dhruv told Kalyani, his mother, and dropped his bag by the door.
Saturday. Cricket in the society park till lunch, cartoons till dinner, then more cricket on the terrace. The bag stayed by the door.
Sunday, 9 pm. Dhruv finally opened the textbook. The cell had eleven parts, and each needed a label and a colour. He did the maths: at least an hour. His chin shook, and then he was sobbing. "Amma, help me, please!" Kalyani sighed, switched off the TV and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: What was Dhruv's weekend task?
qa.a: A labelled diagram of a plant cell.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv sobbing on Sunday night?
qa.a: He felt panicked and overwhelmed when he saw eleven parts needing at least an hour, so late on Sunday.

qa.q: What would have helped on Saturday?
qa.a: Doing the diagram before cricket in the park; 'two whole days' felt like plenty, but it disappeared without a plan.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see Sunday night?
qa.a: Kalyani sighs and switches off the TV, so she seems tired and a bit frustrated, but still chooses to sit with him.

grounding: Illustrates a boy believing he has plenty of time all weekend, then crying at 9 pm on Sunday when the diagram needs an hour.

subtype: Approach: seeing the crowded evening and redoing the plan [Revision]
passage: Tanvir was halfway through his Bengali copying at five when he heard Ammu on the phone: "Yes, come at six, stay for dinner." Cousin Tushar was coming, with his cricket bat, no doubt. Tanvir looked at the plan on his sticky note: copying, then reading, then sums at seven. At seven Tushar would be here, and nobody does sums with a cousin in the room. He crossed out the order and wrote it again: sums now, before they come; reading after they leave. He finished the last sum at 5:55, just as the doorbell rang. At ten, with the Kolkata flat quiet, he read his chapter in bed.

qa.q: What time was Tushar coming?
qa.a: At six, to stay for dinner.

qa.q: What was on Tanvir's mind when he looked at his sticky note?
qa.a: He felt a flash of worry that sums at seven would clash with Tushar's visit, and was determined to fix the plan before then.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir have done if there was no time for the sums before six?
qa.a: He could have asked Ammu for a quiet half-hour during the visit; noticing the clash early is what saved him.

qa.q: How might Tushar's visit be different because of Tanvir's change?
qa.a: Tushar gets a cousin who is free to play, instead of one stuck on sums or worrying about them.

grounding: Shows a boy noticing halfway through his homework that a cousin is visiting at six, moving his sums earlier and reading after the guests leave.

subtype: Approach: seeing the crowded evening and redoing the plan [Revision]
passage:
"Uday, your cousin Anand is coming at six. Bua is bringing him."
"At six?" Uday looked at his notebook. Drawing done. Reading and sums still to go. "I was going to do sums after dinner."
"Dinner will be late. Bua will stay till nine at least."
"And Anand will want to play carrom." Uday chewed his pen. "Okay. New plan. Sums now, before they come. Reading after they go."
"Reading at nine?"
"It's only one chapter. I can read in bed."
At 5:50 he shut the maths notebook. At six Anand burst in holding the carrom striker. At 9:20 Uday read the last page, yawning, and switched off the light.

qa.q: What was Anand holding when he burst in?
qa.a: The carrom striker.

qa.q: Why did Uday chew his pen?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that the visit would squeeze out his sums, and was working out a new order.

qa.q: What made Uday's revised plan work?
qa.a: He moved the harder sums to before the visit, while the house was quiet, and left the short reading for after; he checked the evening before it happened.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Uday's new plan?
qa.a: Mummy only asks 'Reading at nine?', so she seems a little doubtful but willing to let him try, and it works.

grounding: Illustrates a boy seeing a cousin's visit will crowd his evening and reordering his homework so nothing is left undone.

subtype: Approach: working in short blocks with small breaks [Action]
passage: Aadhya, you say you can't sit still for an hour? Neither could your Varun Mama at your age. When I was in Class 6, Ammi bought a white plastic kitchen timer, the ticking kind. She said, 'Twenty minutes of work, then five minutes of whatever your body wants.' So I'd twist it to twenty and do sums till it rang. Then I'd drink water, stretch on the floor, touch my toes, and twist it to five. When it rang again, going back felt easier, because I knew another break was coming. Four rounds, and my homework was done before the dal reached the table. Ammi would pat that timer like it was a pet.

qa.q: What kind of timer did Ammi buy?
qa.a: A white plastic kitchen timer, the ticking kind.

qa.q: Why did going back to work feel easier for young Varun?
qa.a: He felt less trapped and more willing, because he knew another break was coming soon.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the plan work?
qa.a: Using the five minutes to move and drink water, so each twenty-minute block started fresh.

qa.q: How did Ammi seem to feel about the timer?
qa.a: She patted it like a pet, so she seemed pleased and fond of how it made homework calmer.

grounding: Shows a child using a kitchen timer for twenty minutes of work and five minutes of water and stretching, finishing homework before dinner.

subtype: Approach: working in short blocks with small breaks [Action]
passage: Anirban had harmonium practice in the next room, and the same wobbly song kept drifting through the wall. Alka had five sums, a science answer and a spelling list, and dinner was at eight. She went to the kitchen, took the old egg timer and set it for twenty minutes. "Work till it rings," she told herself. She did three sums. Ding. Five minutes: a glass of water, arms up to the ceiling, a peek at Anirban, who stuck his tongue out. Then twenty minutes again: two sums and the science answer. Ding. Water, stretch. The last block was spellings. By 7:45 everything was in her bag.

qa.q: What did Alka do during her breaks?
qa.a: She drank a glass of water, stretched her arms up to the ceiling and peeked at Anirban.

qa.q: What do Alka's words 'Work till it rings' suggest about her mood?
qa.a: She seemed determined and focused despite the wobbly harmonium, using the timer to steady herself.

qa.q: What else could Alka try if the noise got worse?
qa.a: Use a break to ask Anirban to close his door, or move to a quieter spot; the short blocks already made the noise easier to bear.

qa.q: What might the evening be like for Anirban?
qa.a: Anirban gets to practise and tease Alka through the doorway, and probably doesn't know how distracting the song was.

grounding: Illustrates a child working in twenty-minute timed blocks with five-minute water and stretch breaks, finishing before dinner despite noise.

subtype: Approach: working next to a sibling doing their own homework [Action]
passage: Anirban dada had board exams in March, so every evening he sat at the dining table in their Kolkata flat with his chemistry book, pen moving, not talking. Pallavi used to do homework on the bed, where she always ended up reading comics. Tonight she carried her books to the other end of the table. The ceiling fan whirred. Dada scribbled; she wrote. When she wanted to get up, she saw him still bent over his book, and stayed. One sum kept her stuck for a long time. She tried twice, then slid the notebook across. "Dada, just this one?" He showed her in two lines and went back to his chemistry.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi use to do her homework?
qa.a: On the bed, where she always ended up reading comics.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi stay when she wanted to get up?
qa.a: Seeing Anirban still bent over his book made her feel steadier and more motivated to keep going.

qa.q: What else could help Pallavi on nights when Anirban is out?
qa.a: Keep working at the same table and note questions for later; the quiet table seems to be part of what works.

qa.q: How might Anirban see his sister joining him?
qa.a: Anirban helps with one sum in two lines and goes back to work, so he seems fine with her there as long as she only asks when stuck.

grounding: Shows a girl doing homework at the same table as her studying older brother, keeping going and asking only when truly stuck.

subtype: Approach: working next to a sibling doing their own homework [Action]
passage:
"Can I sit here, Bhaiya?"
"If you're quiet. I've got a physics test."
Payal put her Hindi notebook down across from Divyansh. For a while there was only the scratch of two pens.
"Bhaiya, what's-"
"Is it really stuck, or just boring?"
Payal read the question again. "...Boring. Never mind."
She wrote four more answers. Divyansh turned a page. Payal turned a page.
Then: "Bhaiya. This one is really stuck. I tried three times."
He leaned over. "Look, the answer's in paragraph two. Read it again."
"Oh!" She wrote it down. "Thanks."
"Quiet now." But he was smiling.

qa.q: What subject was Divyansh's test in?
qa.a: Physics.

qa.q: What was Payal thinking when she said 'Boring. Never mind'?
qa.a: She realised the question wasn't truly stuck, just dull, and felt a little sheepish about interrupting.

qa.q: What rule could help Payal decide when to ask?
qa.a: Try a question a few times first, as she did before saying 'I tried three times', and only then ask.

qa.q: How does Divyansh seem to feel about Payal sitting with him?
qa.a: He asks for quiet but helps when she's really stuck and ends up smiling, so he seems glad to have her there 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a girl working beside her older brother as he studies, keeping going and asking only when she is truly stuck.

subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Tejas spent the whole evening on one fractions question, rubbing out until the page tore. Four other sums never got done, and he went to bed cross.
Wednesday. Another fractions question: 3/4 of 20. Fifteen minutes passed. Tejas noticed his fists were clenched and he was only getting angrier, not closer. He drew a star beside it, walked to the kitchen and said, "Aai, can you look at the starred one?" Then he went back and did the rest.
Friday. When a question stuck, he starred it after a few tries, asked Aai, and was downstairs playing with Divyansh by six.

qa.q: What happened to the page on Monday?
qa.a: He rubbed out until the page tore.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling after fifteen minutes on Wednesday?
qa.a: He noticed his clenched fists and that he was only getting angrier, not closer, which told him to stop and ask.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Starring the question and asking Aai, then moving on; the other sums got done instead of one question eating the whole evening 👍

qa.q: How might Divyansh notice the change by Friday?
qa.a: Divyansh gets a playmate downstairs by six, instead of Tejas stuck indoors and cross.

grounding: Shows a boy noticing that fifteen minutes on a fractions question is only making him upset, starring it, asking his mother and doing the rest.

subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
passage: Darshan, you've been glaring at that sum for twenty minutes. Let your Pankaj Chacha tell you something. When I was in Class 5, there was one fractions question I could not crack. I sat for fifteen minutes, pencil going round and round, and I noticed I wasn't thinking any more, only getting hot in the face. So I drew a star beside it, like our teacher did on the board for hard ones, and took it to my mother, who was stitching blouses by the window. She showed me in two minutes. And while she threaded her needle again, I did the other six questions. That star saved my evening.

qa.q: What was Pankaj's mother doing when he took the sum to her?
qa.a: She was stitching blouses by the window.

qa.q: What did young Pankaj notice about how he felt after fifteen minutes?
qa.a: He noticed he wasn't thinking any more, only getting hot in the face, which meant he was frustrated and upset.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Drawing a star and asking his mother instead of staring; she explained it in two minutes and he could finish the other six.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother have seen being asked?
qa.a: She showed him in two minutes and went back to her needle, so she probably saw it as a small, easy interruption.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who notices fifteen minutes stuck is only upsetting him, stars the question, asks his mother and carries on.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage:
"Chetan! Cricket! We need a bowler!"
"Two minutes, Darshan!" Chetan scribbled the last sums, closed the notebook with a slap, and ran.
"Did you check them?"
"No time. They're right, I'm sure."
Next morning Mrs Pillai handed back the notebooks.
"Chetan, come here." She tapped the page. "The question says 48. You wrote 84. And here, 306 became 360. Both would be right if you'd copied the numbers properly."
"But I knew how to do them!"
"I know you did. One minute of checking would have caught both."
Chetan stared at the two red marks. At break Darshan asked, "Cricket after school?" Chetan said, "After I check."

qa.q: What number did Chetan write instead of 48?
qa.a: He wrote 84.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he stared at the two red marks?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and disappointed, since he knew how to do the sums and lost marks only for copying errors.

qa.q: What small step would have saved Chetan's marks?
qa.a: One minute of checking each number against the question before closing the notebook, even with Darshan waiting.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Chetan's 'After I check'?
qa.a: Darshan may be a little impatient to play, but gets a friend who comes out without worrying about more red marks.

grounding: Shows a boy rushing his sums to go and play, skipping the check, and losing two sums to copying errors a minute would have caught.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage: I remember the day I learned to check. It was a Tuesday, and the boys from my building were already shouting from the ground below. 'Yusuf, come on!' I had ten sums left. Ammi said, 'Beta, slowly,' but I raced through them, barely looking at the textbook, shut the notebook and ran. Next day Alka Ma'am called me to her desk. Two sums had big red circles. In one I had written 17 where the book said 71. In the other I had copied a plus as a minus. My method was right both times. 'One minute, Yusuf,' she said. 'That's all checking takes.' I was so embarrassed I didn't go down to play that evening.

qa.q: What did Yusuf write instead of 71?
qa.a: He had written 17.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when he saw the red circles?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, enough to skip playing that evening, because his method was right and only copying slips cost him.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do next time the boys are shouting for him?
qa.a: Take one minute to check each answer against the book before running down, just as Alka Ma'am said.

qa.q: How does Alka Ma'am see Yusuf's mistakes?
qa.a: She sees that his method was right and the errors came from rushing, so she points out that checking takes only a minute.

grounding: Illustrates a boy rushing homework to go and play and losing two sums to copying errors that a minute of checking would have caught.
